---
title: "Quiz: gaps, divisions and lineage trees"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Why link in two stages (strict frame-to-frame linking first, then joining segments) instead of one generous frame-to-frame step?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to a generous gate in a crowded frame?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Generous gates in every frame let wrong links compete everywhere. Strict frame-to-frame linking gives short but reliable segments. The second stage only has to decide about the comparatively few segment ends and starts, and it can afford larger gates (for gaps), extra cues (areas for divisions) and alternatives, in one global assignment.
:::

---

**Q2.** A track ends at frame 20; another starts at frame 23 nearby. How many frames were missed? If the gate for one frame is 6 px for a randomly moving object, about how large should the gate be for this gap?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For random motion, distances grow as the square root of time.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Frames 21 and 22 were missed (the jump spans 3 frames). The gate grows as $\sqrt3$: about $6\sqrt3 \approx 10.4$ px.
:::

---

**Q3.** Give three cues, besides distance, that a track ending next to two new starts is a cell division.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Size, brightness, geometry.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The two daughters' areas add up to about the mother's (each about half); the mother is bright and round just before dividing (mitosis); the daughters appear on opposite sides of the mother's last position and move apart.
:::

---

**Q4.** The tracker reports a division, but one frame later the two "daughters" merge again. What probably happened, and how can a rule catch it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which step produced the two objects?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The segmentation cut one cell into two pieces for one frame: a split followed by a merge, a "bubble". A rule such as "a division must be followed by two daughters that stay separate for k frames" removes it, while the graph keeps what was observed.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why should a track that starts at the image border not be counted as a newborn cell?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where was the cell before?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It most likely existed outside the field and moved in. Its start is a border crossing, not a birth; the same holds for tracks that end at the border (not deaths). Record the reason "border" for such starts and ends.
:::

---

**Q6.** In a 48 h movie you measure cell-cycle times only on cells that were born and divided within the movie. Is the mean too high or too low? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which cycles can fit into the movie?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Too low. A cell born late in the movie can only complete a short cycle before the end; long cycles are more often cut off (censored) and therefore missing from the complete ones.
:::

---

**Q7.** The reference has a division of cell M into D1 and D2. The result has M dividing into D1 and X. Count TP, FP and FN for divisions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A division counts only if the mother and both daughters match.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
TP 0, FP 1 (the result's division M → D1, X), FN 1 (the reference's M → D1, D2). One wrong daughter makes the whole division wrong.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* A random walk with step variance $2D\Delta t$ per axis in 2D. Show that the expected squared displacement over $g$ frames is $4Dg\Delta t$, and conclude how a gap gate should grow with $g$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Variances of independent steps add.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The displacement over $g$ frames is the sum of $g$ independent steps; per axis the variances add to $2Dg\Delta t$, and over two axes $E|\Delta\mathbf r_g|^2 = 4Dg\Delta t$. The typical distance grows as $\sqrt g$, so a gate of $k$ standard deviations should be $k\sqrt{2D\Delta t}\sqrt g$ per axis (radius $\propto \sqrt g$).
:::
